Empirical Research Plan: Long-Run Impacts of Head Start

================================================================
1. Identification Strategy
----------------------------------------------------------------
Chosen method: Fuzzy Regression Discontinuity Design (FRD) supplemented by 2SLS.

Why it fits  
• The program’s first-round federal allocation rule funded only counties whose 1960-era child-poverty rate exceeded a legislated threshold (≈ 30 %).  
• Crossing the threshold generated a large jump in the probability that a Head Start center opened and that eligible children actually attended, but did **not** deterministically assign treatment → a **fuzzy** RD.  
• RD is ideal because assignment is as-good-as-random in a small neighborhood around the cutoff, giving us local causal effects with minimal functional-form assumptions.  
• Individual-level outcomes (education, health, earnings) can be linked to county-of-birth poverty rates, allowing first-stage and reduced-form estimates; 2SLS recovers the Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE) of participation.

================================================================
2. Treatment and Control
----------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
Tᵢ = 1 if child i attended a Head Start center in pre-K year (age 3–4).

Instrument / Assignment variable  
Z_c = 1 if county c’s 1960 child-poverty rate ≥ 30 % (the statutory cutoff).

Control group  
Children born in counties with poverty rates just **below** the threshold (Z_c = 0) form the counterfactual.

Running variable & cutoff  
R_c = (child-poverty rate in 1960, %).  
Cutoff c* = 30.0.  
We will work with the centered score: r_c = R_c − 30.

Timing  
Treatment “date” is cohort-specific: first year the program was offered in the county (generally 1965–66). For life-cycle outcomes we use birth-cohort-by-county assignment: r_c and Z_c are measured **pre-program**, eliminating reverse causality.

================================================================
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
----------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff  
   Absent the program, children in counties just above/below 30 % poverty would have had identical expected outcomes.  
   Plausibility: Poverty data were measured before program design; counties could not have foreseen the precise cutoff.

A2. No precise manipulation of the running variable  
   County poverty rates came from the decennial Census; counties cannot manipulate these retrospectively. We will confirm with McCrary density tests.

A3. Exclusion & relevance (for fuzzy RD/IV)  
   Crossing the cutoff affects outcomes *only* via increased access to Head Start; and the first-stage jump in participation is sizable. Federal regulations tied funds almost exclusively to Head Start, supporting exclusion.

A4. Monotonicity  
   Being in an above-threshold county weakly increases one’s chance of attending (no “defiers”). Reasonable because program availability cannot *reduce* attendance.

A5. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA) locally  
   Spillovers across small bandwidth of counties are limited; we will test for cross-county migration.

================================================================
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
----------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Manipulation / bunching of poverty rates  
   • Density (McCrary) and covariate-balance plots around r_c = 0.  
   • Show poverty share was measured before the program and published later, limiting gaming.

T2. Confounding policies linked to poverty cutoff  
   • Collect data on other Great Society programs (Title I, Medicaid rollout) and verify they do *not* jump at 30 %.  
   • If any do, include them as controls or conduct “difference-in-RD” exploiting that Head Start opens in 1965 while other programs started in different years.

T3. Selective migration / attrition  
   • Restrict to individuals who reside in their birth county through age 5 (using Census linkage).  
   • Show continuity in out-migration rates at the cutoff; perform robustness dropping high-mobility counties.

================================================================
5. R Code Outline
----------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# --- 0. Packages --------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)       # fast high-dim IV/RD
library(rdrobust)     # non-parametric RD
library(ggplot2)

# --- 1. Load Data -------------------------------------------------------------
df <- fread("headstart_longrun.csv")   # assumes one row per child

# Key variables expected:
#   y_educ   : years of schooling (adult)
#   y_health : health index (std. dev.)
#   y_earn   : log earnings (age 30–40)
#   hs_part  : 1 if attended Head Start
#   pov1960  : county child-poverty rate in 1960 (%)
#   county   : county FIPS
#   cohort   : birth year
#   X1, X2…  : child/parent covariates

# --- 2. Variable Construction -------------------------------------------------
cutoff <- 30
df[, rscore := pov1960 - cutoff]             # running variable
df[, above  := as.integer(rscore >= 0)]      # assignment
# optional bandwidth: 10 percentage points
bw <- 10
sample <- df[abs(rscore) <= bw]

# --- 3. Main Fuzzy RD / 2SLS --------------------------------------------------
# First-stage: hs_part ~ above + f(rscore)
feols(hs_part ~ above + poly(rscore, 2) | 0, data = sample)

# Second-stage for schooling (local LATE)
mod_educ <- feols(y_educ ~ 1 | 0 | 
                 (hs_part ~ above + poly(rscore, 2)), 
                 data = sample, se = "hc3")
summary(mod_educ)

# Or non-parametric bandwidth/data-driven
rd_out <- rdrobust(y = sample$y_educ,
                   x = sample$rscore,
                   fuzzy = sample$hs_part,
                   c = 0)
summary(rd_out)

# --- 4. Robustness: Vary Bandwidth & Placebo Cutoff --------------------------
for(b in c(5,7.5,10,12.5)){
  sample_b <- df[abs(rscore) <= b]
  cat("\nBandwidth =", b, "\n")
  print(summary(
    feols(y_educ ~ 1 | 0 | (hs_part ~ above + poly(rscore,2)),
          data = sample_b, se = "hc3")))
}

# Placebo at ±5 p.p.
df[, above_placebo := as.integer(rscore >= 5)]
placebo <- feols(y_educ ~ 1 | 0 | (hs_part ~ above_placebo + poly(rscore, 2)),
                 data = df[abs(rscore-5)<=10], se = "hc3")
summary(placebo)
```

================================================================
6. Expected Results
----------------------------------------------------------------
Based on prior literature and human-capital theory:

• Education: +0.2 to +0.4 additional years of schooling (≈ 0.15–0.25 SD).  
• Health: −0.10 SD in adverse health index (better health).  
• Earnings: +5 % to +10 % higher annual earnings in adulthood.

Heterogeneity: Larger gains for girls and for children from the lowest-income households.

================================================================
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)
----------------------------------------------------------------
C1: No manipulation of running variable ………………… 1  
C2: Covariate balance at cutoff …………………………… 1  
C3: Large first-stage / relevance …………………………… 1  
C4: No other discontinuous treatments …………………… 0.5  
C5: Robustness to bandwidth & polynomial choice ………… 1  

Total = 4.5 / 5.
